 Sergei Pavlovich Deserves the Next Heavyweight Title Shot Over Pereira
 Originally posted on
 BoxingNews.com 
  | 
 Last updated Nov 12, 2026 10:42 AM ET
 Add us as a preferred source on Google
 The UFC heavyweight division has a dangerous habit of chasing narratives over merit, and the Alex Pereira hype train represents the latest example. While Pereira's star power is undeniable, Sergei Pavlovich stands as the clearest, most deserving heavyweight title challenger — a knockout artist with legitimate divisional credentials who shouldn't be bypassed for a light heavyweight making his second appearance above 205 pounds.
 Pavlovich's case starts with his power. The Russian heavyweight owns a first-round knockout rate that rivals anyone in UFC history at the weight class. His 2023 tear through the division included devastating finishes of Tai Tuivasa in 54 seconds and Curtis Blaydes in under four minutes. Against Blaydes — a wrestler known for suffocating opponents — Pavlovich needed just one clean combination to end the night. That kind of finishing ability isn't built on gimmicks or crossover appeal; it's heavyweight violence at its purest.
 More importantly, Pavlovich has absorbed the division's lessons. His November 2023 loss to Tom Aspinall wasn't a referendum on his skills — Aspinall is arguably the most well-rounded heavyweight in the sport. The defeat came after Pavlovich had already proven himself against top-ten competition, weathering the pressure of a title eliminator and delivering when it mattered. Compare that resume to Pereira's heavyweight trajectory: one win over a declining Stipe Miocic at UFC 335, however impressive the finish. Miocic hadn't competed in over two years before that bout. A single victory, even a spectacular one, doesn't leapfrog five years of divisional work.
 The counterargument relies on spectacle — Pereira draws eyes, sells pay-per-views, and represents the kind of crossover matchup that casual fans crave. Fair enough. But the UFC heavyweight title isn't supposed to be a promotional tool for building superstars. It's the division's championship, and Pavlovich has earned his place in line through the traditional path: fighting ranked contenders, finishing them violently, and waiting his turn. If Pereira wants the belt, he should prove himself against someone like Pavlovich first — a fight that would test whether his striking translates against an opponent with comparable knockout power and far more heavyweight mileage.
 Pavlovich could reasonably secure a title shot with one more win over a top-five opponent, and the UFC would be wise to book it. The division needs fresh blood at the top, and the Russian heavyweight represents a legitimate threat to any champion. Pereira's time will come if he continues winning, but merit should still matter. Pavlovich has done the work. Give him the shot.
